title: The number in range is the count
idea: range(n) runs the body n times. Change n, change how many repeats. Practice reading and setting the count.

exercises.prompt: range(7) repeats the body how many times?
exercises.explanation: range(7) means seven passes. The number inside range is the repeat count, straight up.

exercises.prompt: To make a loop repeat 10 times, what do you write?
exercises.explanation: range(10) gives ten passes. Want N repeats? Write range(N).

exercises.prompt: Changing range(3) to range(300) makes the body run 300 times instead of 3.
exercises.explanation: One number change scales the repeats from 3 to 300. That's the power loops have over copy-paste.
range(4) = four passes, one X each on its own line — four X lines.
range(8) runs the body eight times. The count lives inside range.

exercises.prompt: Match each range to how many times the body runs.
exercises.explanation: range(n) always runs the body n times. Reading the count is just reading the number.

exercises.prompt: range(1) runs the body how many times?
exercises.explanation: range(1) is a single pass. The loop still works — it just doesn't repeat.

exercises.prompt: You want Hi to show 3 times but wrote range(2). What's the fix?
exercises.explanation: The count is one short, so bump range to 3. The number in range controls repeats.

exercises.prompt: range(0) runs the body zero times — nothing prints.
exercises.explanation: A count of 0 means no passes. Loops handle 'none' without error — a useful edge case to know.

exercises.prompt: A program needs to print a line for each of 50 seats. What range do you use?
exercises.explanation: 50 seats, 50 repeats — range(50). Match the count in range to the number of things.
